The derivation starts from the rate statement −mc dθ/dt = K (θ − θ0). The left side is the heat lost by a body whose temperature is falling, written per unit time.
Divide both sides by (θ − θ0) and by −mc: dθ / (θ − θ0) = −(K/mc) dt. The variables are now separated.
Integrate the left side from the initial temperature θ1 to the later temperature θ, and the right side from t = 0 to t. The integral of dθ/(θ − θ0) is a natural logarithm of the excess.
confusion: Do not integrate θ itself if the denominator is the excess.
The constant K/mc is positive. The minus sign makes the excess shrink.
θ0 is not the integration limit. θ1 is.
An exponential decay does not become a straight line on a θ–t graph.

At t = mc/K the excess is 1/e of its start.
specialNotes: c and K must be constant to come out of the integral.
A change of state would add a latent-heat term.

exercises.question: Show the step from the separated equation to the exponential form.
steps: Integrate both sides between θ1 at t = 0 and θ at time t.
The left side is ln(θ − θ0) − ln(θ1 − θ0).

summary: Separating variables in Newton's law and integrating from the initial excess produces a logarithm. Exponentiating that logarithm gives an exponential decay of the excess temperature toward the room.
